However, challenges remain in achieving cost competitiveness and ensuring broad engine compatibility across the rail fleet. To fully realize the potential of these fuels, future efforts should focus on optimizing production economics, validating emissions and energy performance through real-world demonstrations, and conducting rigorous engine compatibility testing. The following key areas have been identified for further investigation: advanced conversion technologies (Section 7.1), engine compatibility and performance (Section 7.2), fuel blends and optimization (Section 7.3), TEA (Section 7.4), lifecycle and environmental impact assessments (Section 7.5), feedstock availability and supply chain logistics (Section 7.6), technological integration and systems analysis (Section 7.7), regional fuel demand analysis (Section 7.8), and scale-up analysis (Section 7.9). 7.1 ADVANCED CONVERSION TECHNOLOGIES More R&D is needed to explore innovative conversion technologies that can improve the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of producing alternative fuels. This includes developing new catalysts and processes for converting biomass, organic waste, and renewable hydrogen into viable fuel options. Emphasis should be placed on scaling up and demonstrating promising technologies, such as HTL and CFP, to commercial levels. 7.2 ENGINE COMPATIBILITY AND PERFORMANCE Most of the seven fuel categories across sixteen pathways studied in this effort have little performance data from end-use testing on rail engines. RD and BD are drop-in fuels (or nearly drop-in) for existing diesel engines. A high-level screening was completed for the other fuels, some of which would require dual-fuel operation, and to determine whether the fuel would be a promising main or pilot fuel. Ethanol and methanol are not suitable for use as a replacement for diesel fuel, but they could be used in dual-fuel applications with additional modifications to the engine and fuel system. Further studies and demonstrations are needed to understand the compatibility of alternative fuels with existing locomotive engines and to provide emissions factors for these types of studies.
